session.question: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
session.answer:
Textile waste management can adopt a circular waste-to-adsorbent strategy by converting biomass or industrial biowaste into low-cost materials that remove dyes and other contaminants from wastewater. In this approach, waste is first processed into adsorbents such as biochar, activated carbon, nanocellulose composites, or regenerated biomass, then used to capture color, COD (chemical oxygen demand), TDS (total dissolved solids), turbidity, and specific dye molecules from textile effluents. (kalengyo2023utilizingorangepeel chunk 1, reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1, tharayil2023sustainablewastevalorisation chunk 1, holilah2024fabricationasustainable chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

The adsorption performance of these materials depends on high surface area, porosity, mesopores, surface functional groups, and surface charge, which control uptake through physisorption and chemisorption. Examples in the context show Langmuir and Freundlich adsorption behavior, pseudo-second-order kinetics, and high removal efficiencies for dyes such as malachite green, acid blue 9, Rhodamine B, Alizarine red S, and methylene blue. Reusability through adsorption-desorption cycles further improves process sustainability. (reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1, tharayil2023sustainablewastevalorisation chunk 1, holilah2024fabricationasustainable chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

A further circular design is to regenerate spent adsorbents and convert them into energy or carbon products. For example, orange-peel adsorbent can be reused, then co-digested to produce biogas, and the digestate pyrolyzed to biochar. This integrates pollutant removal with resource recovery and reduces secondary waste generation, making textile wastewater treatment more financially and environmentally feasible. (kalengyo2023utilizingorangepeel chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-9fc3601e: The excerpt describes a waste-to-wealth approach where orange peel biomass is used as an adsorbent to treat textile wastewater, removing COD, TDS, turbidity, and color. After adsorption, the spent adsorbent is regenerated and co-digested with cow dung to produce biogas, then the remaining digestate is pyrolyzed to make biochar. This shows a circular textile waste management strategy that combines adsorption-based pollutant removal with subsequent waste conversion into energy and carbon materials, offering an integrated and financially feasible treatment pathway.
From Roice Bwambale Kalengyo, Mona G. Ibrahim, Manabu Fujii, and Mahmoud Nasr. Utilizing orange peel waste biomass in textile wastewater treatment and its recyclability for dual biogas and biochar production: a techno-economic sustainable approach. Biomass Conversion and Biorefinery, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s13399-023-04111-1, doi:10.1007/s13399-023-04111-1.

pqac-e3e1095f: The excerpt describes a 2024 study on converting biomass waste into mesoporous activated carbon (MAC) for wastewater treatment. Using Ficus religiosa leaf biomass, the authors produced MAC with high surface area (480 m2/g) and mesopores around 4 nm. The material effectively adsorbed hazardous dyes acid blue 9 and malachite green, with Langmuir isotherm behavior and pseudo-second-order chemisorption. It also remained reusable for five adsorption-desorption cycles. This suggests textile waste management could benefit by converting waste into adsorbent materials that capture dye pollutants from wastewater, combining waste valorization with treatment.
From Y. Subba Reddy, Naresh Kumar Rotte, B.K. Sudhakar, Navin Chand, Ramavath Janraj Naik, Sudip Mandal, and M. Ravi Chandra. Biomass-derived sustainable mesoporous activated carbon as an efficient and recyclable adsorbent for the adsorption of hazardous dyes. Hybrid Advances, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hybadv.2024.100218, doi:10.1016/j.hybadv.2024.100218.

pqac-81b479c5: The excerpt describes converting agro-waste areca catechu L. husk into biochar via low-rate pyrolysis and using it as an adsorbent for textile wastewater dyes. The biochar’s functional groups, graphite-like carbon structure, and porous morphology support dye adsorption, with high removal efficiencies for Rhodamine B and Alizarine red S. The study shows that waste-to-biochar conversion can create effective adsorbents, and that adsorption performance can be modeled and optimized using response surface methodology, kinetics, and isotherm studies. This suggests textile waste management can leverage converted waste materials to remove dyes and other contaminants from wastewater sustainably.
From Jeevan Mathew Tharayil and Prakash Chinnaiyan. Sustainable waste valorisation: novel areca catechu l. husk biochar for anthraquinone dye adsorption - characterization, modelling, kinetics, and isotherm studies. Results in Engineering, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rineng.2023.101624, doi:10.1016/j.rineng.2023.101624.

pqac-0207f387: The excerpt describes converting biomass waste into a functional adsorbent: nanocellulose was isolated from mangosteen peel waste and combined with mesoporous hectorite and alginate to form beads for methylene blue removal from water. The resulting composite showed strong adsorption performance (up to 98.64% removal, 57.59 mg/g capacity), followed a Freundlich isotherm and PSO kinetics, and was reusable over six cycles. This suggests a general waste-management approach: convert waste into value-added adsorption materials that can capture pollutants in water, reducing both waste and contamination.
From Holilah Holilah, Asranudin Asranudin, Noureddine El Messaoudi, Maria Ulfa, Amir Hamzah, Zuratul Ain Abdul Hamid, Dini Viandi Ramadhani, Lisman Suryanegara, Melbi Mahardika, Alvina Tata Melenia, Agus Wedi Pratama, and Didik Prasetyoko. Fabrication a sustainable adsorbent nanocellulose-mesoporous hectorite bead for methylene blue adsorption. Case Studies in Chemical and Environmental Engineering, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cscee.2024.100850, doi:10.1016/j.cscee.2024.100850.

pqac-bf87d119: The excerpt discusses biochar as a sustainable, low-cost, and environmentally friendly adsorbent made from biowaste for wastewater treatment. It emphasizes that biochar can be produced by converting waste into a useful material and that its adsorption performance depends on properties such as porosity, surface area, surface charge, and functional groups, which can be improved through chemical modification. Although the excerpt focuses on biochar rather than textile waste specifically, the same idea could apply to textile waste management: convert textile waste into value-added adsorbent materials and tune their surface properties to remove pollutants from wastewater.
From Stuti Jha, Rama Gaur, Syed Shahabuddin, and Inderjeet Tyagi. Biochar as sustainable alternative and green adsorbent for the remediation of noxious pollutants: a comprehensive review. Toxics, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/toxics11020117, doi:10.3390/toxics11020117.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes converting agricultural waste (pomegranate peels) into activated carbons using a one-step alkaline carbonate activation process. The resulting carbon materials are highly porous, microporous, and have very high surface area, making them effective adsorbents for CO2 and other gases. This shows how waste conversion can transform low-value biomass into functional adsorbents for environmental and energy applications. By analogy, textile waste management could use similar waste-to-adsorbent conversion approaches to create adsorption materials from textile-derived waste, leveraging porosity and surface area to capture pollutants or gases and support resource recovery.
contexts.question: How can textile waste management use waste conversion and the adsorption properties of textile-derived materials?

The paper also emphasizes environmental concerns from landfill deposition and frames waste conversion as a sustainable route toward a circular textile economy. However, it does not discuss adsorption properties of textile-derived materials or how adsorption might be used in waste management.

Chemical treatments gave the highest adsorption capacities. Although this paper is about orange peels rather than textiles, the relevant idea for textile waste management is that waste can be converted into modified adsorbent materials to capture contaminants, using structural/chemical modification to enhance adsorption performance.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?

Textile waste management can adopt a circular waste-to-adsorbent strategy by converting biomass or industrial biowaste into low-cost materials that remove dyes and other contaminants from wastewater. In this approach, waste is first processed into adsorbents such as biochar, activated carbon, nanocellulose composites, or regenerated biomass, then used to capture color, COD (chemical oxygen demand), TDS (total dissolved solids), turbidity, and specific dye molecules from textile effluents. (kalengyo2023utilizingorangepeel chunk 1, reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1, tharayil2023sustainablewastevalorisation chunk 1, holilah2024fabricationasustainable chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

The adsorption performance of these materials depends on high surface area, porosity, mesopores, surface functional groups, and surface charge, which control uptake through physisorption and chemisorption. Examples in the context show Langmuir and Freundlich adsorption behavior, pseudo-second-order kinetics, and high removal efficiencies for dyes such as malachite green, acid blue 9, Rhodamine B, Alizarine red S, and methylene blue. Reusability through adsorption-desorption cycles further improves process sustainability. (reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1, tharayil2023sustainablewastevalorisation chunk 1, holilah2024fabricationasustainable chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

A further circular design is to regenerate spent adsorbents and convert them into energy or carbon products. For example, orange-peel adsorbent can be reused, then co-digested to produce biogas, and the digestate pyrolyzed to biochar. This integrates pollutant removal with resource recovery and reduces secondary waste generation, making textile wastewater treatment more financially and environmentally feasible. (kalengyo2023utilizingorangepeel chunk 1)
